## Chapter Summary

SQL lets an auditor test entire populations across the tables of a process, and a population test finds the actual exceptions rather than an error rate. Its power depends on its inputs, so every test begins by reconciling the population to the ledger, remembering that two records on the same basis can agree and still omit the same thing, and by profiling it: its records, its dates, and the entries incomplete from the start. The source-document columns of the ledger allow a trace in two directions. An anti-join from the ledger to a document table finds postings with no document, which tests existence and contributes to testing the occurrence of the recorded transactions, and an anti-join from the documents to the ledger finds recorded documents never posted, which tests completeness. Neither proves that the event occurred or finds a transaction omitted from both records. UNION ALL combines the results of several tests into one labeled list of exceptions, matching their columns by position. A cutoff test compares the posting date with the date of the event behind it: the delivery of the goods for revenue, when control passes on delivery, and the work of the pay period for payroll.

A three-way match compares the quantities ordered, received, and invoiced at the level of the purchase order line, after the receipts and invoices of each line are summed, and it compares invoice prices with order prices within a tolerance chosen in advance. Goods received but not yet invoiced are an accrual, and their value should agree with the ledger. Approval tests join each document to its approver and compare it with the approver's limit, employment dates, and role, and with the document's creator, and they also reveal how concentrated the approval of a process is. Tests of the records behind a cost reconcile the chain from the time clock through the labor record and the payroll register to the payment and the ledger, and then test each link. A substantive analytical procedure compares a recorded amount with an expectation built from a plausible relationship in other data, such as revenue or commissions predicted from other measures, and investigates differences above a threshold set in advance. Recalculating the pay for the hours at each employee's rate on file is a recalculation, which supports the arithmetic of the pay on those inputs but not that the hours were worked. Isolated exceptions usually show a control that did not operate; systematic patterns more often show one that is missing or poorly designed. Chapter 8's aging, stratification, duplicate, sequence, and first-digit tests translate into CASE, GROUP BY, self-joins, LAG, and aggregates, and a documented library of such tests can be rerun every period.

Applied to the audit committee's questions, the tests found that the populations tested reconcile to the ledger and that the traces found only six postings without a document, but that revenue and payroll are recorded when invoiced and paid, so each year-end is misstated and the wages of late December are never accrued. The six postings that do not trace record cash paid without a payment record, two of those payments for an employee who had left. The purchasing chain matches, and its unbilled receipts agree with the ledger, but its approvals show exceptions and a single point of failure. The manufacturing hours were clocked, recorded, and paid at the rates on file, and the months of 2024 with little indirect time are recorded like the others, while the plant was building stock, a plausible explanation still to confirm. The payroll exceptions are small but reach manufacturing. The most important finding is that the growth in overtime sits on surge days, on which every hourly manufacturing employee clocked the same hours, approved by one manager and mostly charged to operations that had already ended, so those hours need corroboration before the committee relies on the explanation of where they went. These tests give no reason to revise the standards, though they do not show that the standards are right. In the records, the variance grew with the hours paid beyond the recorded work for about the same output, although the tests alone cannot show how much work that output required or how much of the extra time was avoidable.
